newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Big Australia iron venture to float.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Big Australia iron venture to float.

text.p: The big AUSI Ltd direct reduced iron (DRI) plant to be built in Western Australia's Pilbara region is likely to be floated on the Australian Stock Exchange next year, chairman Sir Russel Madigan said on Wednesday.

Further progress would be necessary on the A$1 billion-plus 3.6 million tonnes a year plant before final decisions were taken on the float, he told Reuters. "(It) could probably (be) floated sometime during the construction period," he said.
Construction of the big Mt Anketel plant, 15 km west of Cape Lambert, is planned to start next year, with production slated to begin in the third quarter of 1999 to supply Asian markets.

Madigan's comments followed an AUSI announcement on Monday that the project was forging ahead, that Norweigan construction contracting group Kvaerner ASA had been brought in as a shareholder, and that AUSI was poised to become Western Australia's next iron ore product processor and exporter.
A float could go ahead in 1997 or 1998, but details remained to be ironed out, Madigan told Reuters.
"The project's going to cost well over A$1 billion and that's got to be raised at financial closing," Madigan said.
After financial closing, the prospect was for project shareholders to then raise public funding, he said.
Madigan also said the entry of Kvaerner as a shareholder had involved it contributing only A$2 million so far to progress the feasibility study of the project.
This would give it a stake of less than 20 percent in AUSI, which has so far issued only A$12 million in shares, he said.

Kvaerner was on an equal stakeholder footing with Mobil Corp subsidiary Ampolex Ltd and German steelmaker Georgsmarienhutte, which had both taken up A$2 million worth of shares, he said. Various private investors, including Madigan and other founding interests, hold the remaining shares.

AUSI's three founding directors are Madigan, widely regarded as the prime mover in the development of the Western Australia iron ore industry, Sir Roderick Carnegie, a leading figure in the deregulation of gas in the state and economist Ross Garnaut, a former Australian Ambassador to China.

Madigan said Kingstream Resources NL's A$1.4 billion iron and steel project, also planned for the Pilbara region, might be "a bit behind the eight ball" if it was just beginning technical, economic, financial and environmental feasibility studies into the Western Australia government's preferred site at Oakajee, 25 km north of Geraldton.
"That (feasibility work) took us about two years," he said.
The state government issued a statement on Tuesday naming Oakajee as its preferred site for the Kingstream slab steel project, to be established in conjunction with Taiwan's An Feng Steel Co Ltd.
This was subject to feasibility studies into the site and a deep water port proving acceptable, the statement said.
AUSI had all its approvals and had virtually completed its aboriginal compensation agreement, Madigan said.
There was room for many new iron projects in the Pilbara and Kingstream's project was not seen as a direct competitor of AUSI's DRI venture, he addded.
This was despite the fact that both ventures would be producing metal for the Asian steel industry, he said.
AUSI's DRI processing plant will be the biggest in the world at 3.6 million tonnes annual capacity. -- Sydney 61-2 9373-1800
